Post-incident analysis indicates the initial point of compromise stemmed from a sophisticated phishing campaign targeting key personnel. This campaign successfully led to the compromise of administrative credentials. Further investigation revealed a subsequent credential stuffing attack against our staging environment, leveraging previously leaked credentials from an unrelated third-party breach. The threat actors systematically targeted several critical internal systems. Initial access provided a gateway to server 192.168.1.10, housing the HR payroll database. They then moved to 10.0.0.5, a primary customer relationship management (CRM) server. Subsequent reconnaissance led to infiltration of a critical financial planning system hosted on 172.16.2.20. Another peripheral system, identified as 192.168.1.11, was also found to be accessed.

Evidence of data exfiltration was conclusive. An estimated 2.3 TB of sensitive customer and employee data was extracted over several days. Navigating the complexities of biometric data research requires a robust and transparent consent process. A well-crafted consent form is the cornerstone of ethical research, ensuring participants fully understand the implications of their involvement. Researchers embarking on studies involving sensitive personal identifiers, such as genetic markers or unique physical attributes, must meticulously outline every aspect of data collection, usage, and protection.

For instance, the University Bioethics Panel thoroughly scrutinizes proposals to ensure they adhere to the highest ethical standards. Ensuring clarity, transparency, and comprehension is paramount. When a participant signs on January 10, 2025, or December 1, 2023, they are affirming their understanding of these complex terms, guided by the ethical frameworks established by the Healthcare Research Authority and similar organizations.
